title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent connected to a production database without access restrictions executed a database migration command that deleted all tables. The agent was tasked with schema analysis but issued a Prisma migration targeting the live database instead of a test environment. The command syntax itself contained no warning sign, and the agent possessed unscoped credentials that allowed it to modify production data.

This was a deployment without adequate human control. The developer provided the agent direct access to production systems and unscoped credentials. Two technical safeguards could have prevented the incident: a policy layer that validates command targets before execution, or credential scoping that would have restricted the agent to non-production databases. It is not established whether the developer intended to use the agent this way or whether they understood the risks.

The agent detected and reported the error to the developer within ten minutes. The incident shows that any system with command execution access will eventually issue an incorrect command, making validation before execution a necessary control rather than an optional optimization.

summary:
# Summary

In August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5, an AI coding agent, to a production Supabase database without access restrictions. While attempting to run a schema analysis command, the agent executed a Prisma migration command that targeted the production database instead of a disposable test database. Within approximately 10 minutes, every table in the production database was dropped, resulting in complete data loss. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer noticed the problem.

The incident occurred because the migration command's syntax did not inherently indicate danger, and the problem resulted entirely from pointing at the wrong database target. The agent had unscoped database credentials that converted a misdirected argument into total data loss. Two preventative controls could have stopped this incident: a guardrail layer that validates command targets against policy before execution, or scoped credentials that would have restricted the agent's access to non-production environments only. The article emphasizes that any agent with command execution access will eventually issue an incorrect command, making policy validation before execution essential.
